text: Energy auditing: practical foundations and certification-oriented study

This offline guide explains how to plan an energy audit, calculate basic results, and evaluate practical choices. Inferred means an illustrative example. Added context means information checked outside the supplied materials. Not verified means unconfirmed. For conflicting evidence, open What We Are Not Sure About.
It is for adult beginners learning facility energy auditing and related technical decisions.
You need a calculator, pencil, and basic arithmetic. You do not need technical software or an internet connection.
You will be able to read common energy figures, work through simple audit calculations, recognize likely opportunities, and explain uncertainty.
Allow about 15 to 25 minutes per chapter. Short practice activities need only a few minutes.

Read Level 1 before the other levels. Answer each question before revealing the explanation. Complete a short activity when its linked chapter is clear. Open My Progress to save an export before changing the file or browser.

items: Convert all energy to one unit before adding.
Benchmark similar uses on the same basis.
Verify required service before reducing equipment hours.
Separate electric energy savings from demand savings.
Treat simple payback as screening, not full finance.
Check current examination conditions with the exam provider before relying on dated study outlines.

text: A useful recommendation starts with measured conditions, states uncertainties, and protects required service and safety.

Begin with the owner's question and a clear audit scope. Gather meter records and operational evidence, then describe normal use in a baseline. Examine when and why major systems consume energy. Calculate a credible change, evaluate cost, document limitations, and verify the result after implementation.

items: Scope and records lead to an audit baseline.
Energy units and bills lead to energy-cost calculations.
Schedules and equipment performance lead to candidate measures.
Data checks and risk limits lead to a qualified report.
Verification compares later operation with the adjusted baseline.
